One thing I genuinely enjoy about software development is taking an idea and turning it into something people can actually use. 

That's what I set out to do with Nath ResellDesk.

ResellDesk is a ticket reseller management application I built to make everyday business activities easier. It helps users manage ticket inventory, record sales, monitor revenue and profit, track events, and receive notifications.

Building this project involved more than writing code. I worked on the interface, authentication, browser-based data storage, serverless functions, email delivery, notification integrations, deployment, and debugging.

Here is the actual technology stack behind ResellDesk:

🔹 Frontend

- HTML5
- CSS3 (CSS Variables, Grid, Flexbox and Media Queries)
- Vanilla JavaScript (ES Modules)
- Google Fonts (DM Sans and Plus Jakarta Sans)
- Browser APIs (IndexedDB, localStorage, Fetch API and HTML Dialog)

🔹 Authentication

- Supabase Auth
- supabase-js 2.45.4

🔹 Data Storage

- IndexedDB (ResellDeskDB) for locally storing tickets and sales records in each user's browser
- localStorage for saving theme preferences

🔹 Backend and Notifications

- Netlify Functions
- Node.js
- esbuild
- Resend for email delivery
- Telegram Bot API
- Discord Webhooks

🔹 Hosting and Deployment

- Netlify
- GitHub
- Netlify Environment Variables
- Automatic deployment from GitHub

🔹 Development Tools

- Visual Studio Code
- Git
- GitHub
- Netlify CLI
- "netlify dev" for local development and testing

A few technical details worth mentioning:

ResellDesk uses Vanilla JavaScript. There is no React, no frontend framework and no build step.

Supabase handles authentication, while IndexedDB stores ticket and sales records locally in each user's browser. Cloud synchronisation is not currently implemented.

Netlify hosts the application and serverless notification function, while Resend handles email delivery through a verified domain. Telegram and Discord are used for administrator alerts.

I'm sharing this project because I want people to see not just the finished application, but also the technologies, engineering decisions and practical development skills behind it.

I'm constantly learning, building and improving my craft as a Full-Stack Software Engineer.

Indonesia is looking to unlock its vast forest carbon potential by accessing international compliance carbon markets under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.

At COP31, Indonesian government officials and carbon market experts discussed how demand from Singapore, Japan and the international aviation sector could create new opportunities for the country's forestry and nature-based solutions (NbS) projects.

According to BloombergNEF 2025 data cited by Indonesia's Ministry of Forestry, the country's forest carbon potential is estimated at 13.4 gigatonnes of CO₂.

Where could international demand come from?

→ Singapore: Companies can use eligible international carbon credits to offset up to 5% of their taxable emissions.

→ Japan: Its Joint Crediting Mechanism (JCM) has a cumulative international mitigation target of around 100 million tonnes of CO₂ by 2030 across partner countries. Indonesia is exploring peatland and mangrove projects under this cooperation.

→ ICAO-CORSIA: The international aviation scheme is estimated to require 200–250 million eligible carbon units through January 2028.

Indonesia is building its regulatory framework

The country has introduced Presidential Regulation No. 110/2025 and Forestry Ministerial Regulation No. 6/2026 to support international carbon trading.

These regulations cover the authorisation of Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes (ITMOs), forestry carbon trading procedures and safeguards against double counting.

However, experts highlighted several challenges:

→ Maintaining high environmental and social integrity in forest carbon projects.

→ Ensuring international credit transfers remain consistent with Indonesia's national climate targets.

→ Addressing technical issues around permanence and standardised methodologies under Article 6.4.

→ Providing long-term demand certainty for project developers while giving buyers confidence in credit supply.

The discussions also highlighted the potential to use existing Verra methodologies for REDD+, afforestation and forest protection to accelerate project development.

Indonesia's forest carbon opportunity is significant. Its ability to convert that potential into internationally recognised credits will depend on credible accounting, strong governance, clear regulations and sustained buyer demand.

Source: Petromindo

From "Zero Waste" to Waste-to-Energy: Finding the Pragmatic Equilibrium for Indonesia’s Metropolitan Cities

Across Jakarta, Surabaya, Bandung, Medan, and Makassar, public policy debates on urban waste frequently polarize into two rigid camps: purist "Zero Waste" advocates pushing exclusively for upstream recycling, and infrastructure developers promoting large-scale Waste-to-Energy (WtE) incineration. Yet Indonesia’s metropolitan reality demands engineering pragmatism over ideology. 

Even under aggressive source-separation and recycling programs, megacities generate tens of thousands of tons of non-recyclable residual waste daily—contaminated packaging films, multi-layer plastics, and degraded organics—while legacy open dumpsites approach catastrophic capacity limits. 

Treating upstream circularity and downstream thermal/RDF energy recovery as mutually exclusive stalls urgently needed capital deployment. 

From an energy investment origination and enterprise risk governance perspective, metropolitan WtE infrastructure achieves institutional financial close only when integrated upstream sorting/recycling cascades, right-sized residual energy recovery, and bankable municipal payment structures are engineered upfront.

Six core pillars define institutional origination for achieving a pragmatic Zero-Waste-to-WtE equilibrium in Indonesian cities:

 1. Cascading Material Recovery Facility (MRF) & RDF Integration: Deploying automated upstream MRFs extracts high-value metals, rigid plastics, and clean organics first—routing only genuinely non-recyclable, high-calorific residuals to Refuse-Derived Fuel (RDF) kilns or WtE boilers.

 2. Seasonal Moisture & Calorific Right-Sizing: Designing thermal and biological-drying pre-treatment capacity around Indonesia’s wet-season organic surge prevents boiler underperformance and eliminates excessive fossil co-firing.

 3. Flexible Minimum Tonnage Clauses (Avoiding Feedstock Hunger): Structuring municipal tipping fee (BLPS) contracts with modular capacity bands—rather than rigid punitive tonnage floors—protects city recycling mandates while preserving lender debt-service coverage ratios (DSCR).

 4. Bankable Municipal Tipping Fee & IIGF Credit Enhancement:** Backing regional budget (APBD) availability payments with Indonesia Infrastructure Guarantee Fund (PII/IIGF) wraps and escrow accounts insulates sponsors from political-cycle payment delays.

 5. Continuous Emissions Monitoring (CEMS) & Inclusive Informal-Sector Integration: Pairing real-time public dioxin/particulate telemetry with formal cooperative contracts for existing waste pickers builds durable community social license.

 6. Clean Municipal Concession Tenure & Zero-Tolerance ABAC Controls: Securing unencumbered land/concession validity, Ministry of KLHK technical approvals, and uncompromising ABAC governance protects institutional credit committees.

Every off-plan project looks stunning now.

Renders have got so good that I've stood on building sites in Indonesia holding a brochure, and for a moment I couldn't tell which one was real. The morning light hitting the infinity pool. The perfectly placed frangipani. The couple who will never be seen again.

Here's the uncomfortable truth: you are not buying the render. You're buying the contract.

If the contract doesn't say what the villa is made of, who designed it and who builds it, then the brochure is just a very expensive mood board. And the developer is free to deliver something that is "broadly similar".

Before any of our clients sign, we want to see these written into the contract, or its annexes:

🔹 A full specification sheet: materials, finishes, fixtures and furniture
🔹 Signed floor plans
🔹 The common facilities promised, with a target opening date
🔹 The architect and the interior designer, so you can visit their past work
🔹 The builder, and what they've delivered before
🔹 The operator who will run it after completion, because that's who decides your rental income for the next 20 years

If those names and documents aren't in the paperwork, they aren't part of your purchase.

A beautiful video costs a developer a few thousand dollars. A clear, specific contract costs them commitment. Only one of those protects you.

Buy the contract, not the brochure.

🚗 THE AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY DOESN'T NEED ANOTHER GREEN MATERIAL.
IT NEEDS A MATERIAL THAT PASSES THE TEST.

For automotive manufacturers, choosing a material is not simply about where it comes from. It is about how it performs inside a component.
Mechanical properties. Thermal behavior. Moisture resistance. Durability. Processability. Batch consistency. Every requirement matters.

🥥 THIS IS WHERE COCOFIBER ENTERS THE MATERIAL-ENGINEERING CONVERSATION.
Researchers have investigated coir-fiber-reinforced polypropylene composites for potential automotive applications.

But there is an important distinction:
RAW COCOFIBER IS NOT AN AUTOMOTIVE COMPONENT. IT IS A POTENTIAL REINFORCEMENT MATERIAL.
Its performance depends on much more than the fiber itself.

Several factors influence the final composite:
📏 Fiber length and geometry — influence reinforcement behavior.
🧪Fiber preparation and treatment — can affect surface characteristics and fiber–matrix interaction.
⚙️Fiber–polymer compatibility — influences bonding within the composite.
📊Fiber loading and distribution — affect the material's overall properties.
🏭Processing conditions and composite structure — influence consistency and final performance.

🔬AND THE RESEARCH IS WORTH PAYING ATTENTION TO.
A 2024 life-cycle assessment published in the Journal of Cleaner Production compared a defined coir-fiber-reinforced polypropylene component with a comparable glass-fiber-reinforced polypropylene component.
In that particular study, the coir-based composite showed lower cumulative energy demand and greenhouse gas emissions within the assessed system boundaries.
That is promising evidence.

At CocoHeroBorneo, we believe cocofiber deserves to be explored beyond conventional applications—as a potential raw material for the next generation of natural-fiber composite development.

I've been into motorsport for a long time. I've been sim racing since 2010, and I go karting and do the odd track day. None of it is serious, I just love it.

My son is a different story. He races junior karts, and he only started taking it seriously after we moved to Malaysia. There are far more good tracks here than we had in Indonesia, and the racing is tougher, with drivers from all over the world on the same grid. He's won several events since then, and now he wants to make a career of it.

At that level, small margins decide results. So I need to track how he's driving from one session to the next. How hard is he braking into Turn 1? How much speed does he carry through the hairpin? Where does the three tenths to the kid in front go?

The tools for this have existed for years. AiM's Race Studio 3 is the gold standard for performance analysis, and professional teams also use MoTeC i2. Both are very good. But they need a Windows laptop, each one only reads its own logger's files, and they're built for race engineers. None of that helps when you're standing under a pit tent with ten minutes until the next heat. The GPS data from his GoPro was even harder to use, because the tools wanted the whole multi-gigabyte video uploaded first.

I've worked in software for over 20 years, so at some point I thought, why not build something that fits how we actually use it? I have a full-time job, so I built it at night and on the weekends we weren't at the track.

That became FLATOUT. It runs in a browser and reads files from cameras, loggers and lap timers from different brands. It puts his laps side by side so we can see where he lost time, corner by corner. It isn't meant to replace the pro tools. It's for the driver, the parent and the coach, who aren't race engineers.

I wrote up why I built it and the engineering behind it, including the parts that were much harder than I expected:

https://lnkd.in/gSVjX5NE

I'll keep sharing what I learn as I build it, including what works on track and what doesn't.

Indonesia just joined a list no engineer wants to be on.
Nvidia has told Dell and Supermicro to stop shipping AI servers to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand. The cause is a new US export rule, effective 19 November, that requires a licence for advanced chips sent to these countries. Washington wants to stop Chinese firms renting compute from data centres here instead of importing chips directly.
For most people this sounds like geopolitics. For engineers it is a supply chain problem. The servers that train and run the models your product depends on now need paperwork that did not exist two weeks ago. Dell and Supermicro have already told buyers in the four countries their orders cannot ship, and nobody knows yet if the pause is temporary.
I build AKSARA in Bekasi on Google Gemini APIs, Go and PostgreSQL. I do not own a GPU rack, and this week reminded me that is exactly the point. When you build on someone else's hardware, someone else's licence or someone else's cloud, you need to know what breaks first if that supplier stops answering.
Audit your dependencies like they can disappear tomorrow. Because this week, for four countries, they did.

Thank you CNBC Indonesia & MbakShafinaz Nachiar for hosting me on Monday's Profit Tech a Look. This one means a lot to the wholeSarana team, & I'm grateful for the chance to share what we've been learning on the ground deploying AI across 20 industries in Southeast Asia.

We started Sarana on the tenet that AI should close the productivity delta, rather than feed the usual doom-&-gloom labour-efficiency narrative. After all, when enterprises become more productive, they tend to need more people, not fewer. 

Our job is to give the most precious commodity of all back to the people on the frontlines powering our economy: time. Some numbers that shape our thinking:

• Of the roughly 5% we grow today, about 2.5 points come from capital, 1.6 from labour & only around 1 from productivity (Ministry of Finance)
• For the 8% target, Bank Indonesia estimates productivity's contribution needs to triple, to about 3.6 points a year through 2029
• With an ICOR of around 6, every Rp 1 of extra output still takes about Rp 6 of investment, so capital alone may not carry us there

So the gap has to close through what every working hour produces, & that is where we believe AI earns its place: helping the same people get more done in the same day, & go home on time.

We also believe this work doesn't require anyone to leave home. Our engineering base is in Malang, where some of East Java's most talented young engineers build careers close to their families & deploy wherever the work is: hospital wards, factory floors, mines, bank branches across the country.

We are nothing without the trust of our shareholders, customers & partners, & of course the talented people who have taken a bet on building with us. We are beyond grateful.

14 days ago I started a project on my own: an AI video content production app, plus a knowledge hub for the team. Both are now in production, with 211 deploys and 355 commits behind them.
 
I didn't write all that code myself. I built a team, and the team is 22 AI agents running in Claude Code.
 
It works like a real team:
 
• A lead agent turns my requests into tasks, hands each one to the right agent, checks the result, and deploys.
 • Every agent has its own role brief: frontend, backend, QA, server ops, security reviewer, release checker, product owner, product manager, tech writer, plus a content team (creative director, writer, social media, data engineer, reviewer).
 • Work runs in 4 fixed lanes so two agents never edit the same file. Releases go out twice a day, and every deploy has a rollback point.
 • Anything that touches sign-in, money, or tokens goes through security review before QA.
 
The numbers for those 14 days:
 
• 10.1 billion tokens processed. 97% of them were cache reads, which is why it stays affordable.
 • At Anthropic's API list prices that is about $4,040, or roughly IDR 74 million.
 • 20 software engineers in Jakarta at the median salary (Levels.fyi, IDR 235.7M a year) would cost about IDR 181 million for the same 14 days.
 
So the tokens came to about 40% of what a 20-person engineering payroll costs, before hiring, onboarding, laptops, and office space.
 
My job changed. I don't write code line by line anymore. I decide what gets built, I write the rules, and I keep the decisions an AI should not make on its own: spending, releases, and content policy. The rules are written once, and every agent follows them.
 
It does not run itself. Without clear rules, layered review, and a human at the key decision points, you get speed and a mess.
 
For fellow IT managers: I think the question is no longer "can AI write code?" It is "how do we manage a team made of AI?"

From "Zero Waste" to Waste-to-Energy: Finding the Pragmatic Equilibrium for Indonesia’s Metropolitan Cities

Across Jakarta, Surabaya, Bandung, Medan, and Makassar, public policy debates on urban waste frequently polarize into two rigid camps: purist "Zero Waste" advocates pushing exclusively for upstream recycling, and infrastructure developers promoting large-scale Waste-to-Energy (WtE) incineration. Yet Indonesia’s metropolitan reality demands engineering pragmatism over ideology. 

Even under aggressive source-separation and recycling programs, megacities generate tens of thousands of tons of non-recyclable residual waste daily—contaminated packaging films, multi-layer plastics, and degraded organics—while legacy open dumpsites approach catastrophic capacity limits. 

Treating upstream circularity and downstream thermal/RDF energy recovery as mutually exclusive stalls urgently needed capital deployment. 

From an energy investment origination and enterprise risk governance perspective, metropolitan WtE infrastructure achieves institutional financial close only when integrated upstream sorting/recycling cascades, right-sized residual energy recovery, and bankable municipal payment structures are engineered upfront.

Six core pillars define institutional origination for achieving a pragmatic Zero-Waste-to-WtE equilibrium in Indonesian cities:

 1. Cascading Material Recovery Facility (MRF) & RDF Integration: Deploying automated upstream MRFs extracts high-value metals, rigid plastics, and clean organics first—routing only genuinely non-recyclable, high-calorific residuals to Refuse-Derived Fuel (RDF) kilns or WtE boilers.

 2. Seasonal Moisture & Calorific Right-Sizing: Designing thermal and biological-drying pre-treatment capacity around Indonesia’s wet-season organic surge prevents boiler underperformance and eliminates excessive fossil co-firing.

 3. Flexible Minimum Tonnage Clauses (Avoiding Feedstock Hunger): Structuring municipal tipping fee (BLPS) contracts with modular capacity bands—rather than rigid punitive tonnage floors—protects city recycling mandates while preserving lender debt-service coverage ratios (DSCR).

 4. Bankable Municipal Tipping Fee & IIGF Credit Enhancement:** Backing regional budget (APBD) availability payments with Indonesia Infrastructure Guarantee Fund (PII/IIGF) wraps and escrow accounts insulates sponsors from political-cycle payment delays.

 5. Continuous Emissions Monitoring (CEMS) & Inclusive Informal-Sector Integration: Pairing real-time public dioxin/particulate telemetry with formal cooperative contracts for existing waste pickers builds durable community social license.

 6. Clean Municipal Concession Tenure & Zero-Tolerance ABAC Controls: Securing unencumbered land/concession validity, Ministry of KLHK technical approvals, and uncompromising ABAC governance protects institutional credit committees.

Sometimes, the best ideas come from problems we experience ourselves

With the theme "A Gift for Indonesia", we spent a month working on this project at Apple Developer Academy @ UC, Jakarta, hoping to create something meaningful for the people around us.
 
Instead of looking too far, we started by looking at our own daily lives.
 
As a group of anak kos, we often experienced the same thing: buying groceries, planning to cook, getting busy, and eventually forgetting about the ingredients until they went bad in the fridge. It might seem like a small problem, but we realized that food waste is something we could start addressing through our own everyday habits.
 
After learning more about food waste in Indonesia, we decided to turn this experience into something useful. And that's where Habisin began.
 
Habisin is an iOS app that helps people manage groceries, keep track of expiration dates, and find recipe ideas using ingredients they already have.
 
I worked on this project as a Product Designer & Project Manager.

As a Product Designer, I focused on creating an easy-to-use experience, from designing user flows and wireframes to building prototypes and final UI designs. I also worked on the app's visual consistency, making sure each feature felt simple and easy to navigate. As a Project Manager, I helped organize tasks, set priorities, track progress, and keep the team aligned throughout the process.
 
It wasn't always smooth. We had different ideas, technical challenges, and tight deadlines. But learning to adjust, communicate, and make decisions together was one of the most valuable parts of this experience.
 
One of my favorite moments was presenting Habisin with Mentari Tika in front of experienced professionals. I was nervous and excited at the same time, but the feedback we received gave us new perspectives on our work.

And now, Habisin is officially available on the App Store! 🎉
It's amazing to see an idea that started from our everyday experiences become a real product.
 
I'm grateful to have shared this journey withMichael Geraldi, Audy Hema, Mentari Tika Fortherina Tarigan, Aura Jatra Ratu Semendawai, and Gusti Ngurah Deva Wirandana Putra. Thank you for all the ideas, discussions, feedback, and hard work. Also, a big thank you to our mentors and everyone at Apple Developer Academy for their support!
 
If you often forget about groceries in your fridge too, give Habisin a try!
